HVAC Boot Camp · Unit 1

How air conditioning moves heat

Development review · Progress is not recorded
1Cooling2Heat3State4Sensible/latent5Pressure

Before you begin

No formulas. Follow what the heat and refrigerant are doing.

By the end of this unit, you should be able to explain why an air conditioner moves heat instead of creating cold, how refrigerant absorbs and releases heat, and why pressure changes where refrigerant boils and condenses.

About 20 minutesFive short lessonsPractice without hard grading
Lesson 1 of 5

What cooling really means

Cooling does not mean making cold. It means removing heat.

RETURN AIR78°F

Warmer indoor air

→
EVAPORATOR COIL45°F

Colder coil and refrigerant

Heat naturally moves from warmer material toward cooler material. Because the indoor air is warmer than the evaporator coil, heat moves from the air into the coil and refrigerant. The air leaves with less heat, so it feels cooler.

The system did not add cold.It removed some of the air’s heat and carried it elsewhere.

Which way will heat move?

Lesson 2 of 5

Temperature and thermal energy

Temperature tells part of the story—not the total amount of heat.

Watch for: Heat is energy in motion, and it moves from warmer material toward cooler material.

One cup · 80°F

Less water to cool

One bucket · 80°F

More water to cool

The cup and bucket have the same temperature, but the bucket contains much more water. It requires more heat removal to cool it by the same number of degrees. HVAC technicians use Btu to describe an amount of heat, but you do not need a Btu calculation here.

Both start at 80°F. Which requires more heat removal to reach 70°F?

Lesson 3 of 5

Refrigerant changes state

It remains refrigerant while changing between liquid and vapor.

LIQUIDBoiling absorbs heat

Inside the evaporator, liquid refrigerant absorbs heat and becomes vapor.

⇄
VAPORCondensing releases heat

Inside the condenser, refrigerant vapor releases heat and becomes liquid.

Think about boiling water. Liquid water becomes water vapor, but it is still water. Refrigerant behaves the same way; the system controls the conditions where the change happens.

Liquid refrigerant enters the evaporator and leaves as vapor. What happened?

Lesson 4 of 5

Sensible and latent heat

This is the key to understanding the refrigeration cycle.

Sensible heatChanges temperature

You can follow it with a thermometer.

Latent heatChanges state

Heat moves while temperature remains nearly steady.

Watch for: The thermometer rises until the water boils. Heat keeps entering after the temperature stops rising.

Try it

Watch what the added heat actually does.

BURNER550°FWATER74°F
STEP 1 OF 4

Heat starts entering the water

The burner is hotter than the water, so heat moves into the water.

Water boils at approximately 212°F at normal atmospheric pressure.

The water is boiling at 212°F while more heat is added. Where is the energy going?

Lesson 5 of 5

Pressure makes refrigeration possible

Changing pressure changes the temperature where refrigerant boils and condenses.

INDOORS · EVAPORATORLower pressureLower boiling temperature

Refrigerant can boil cold enough to absorb heat from warmer indoor air.

PRESSURE↓↑controls saturation temperature
OUTDOORS · CONDENSERHigher pressureHigher condensing temperature

Refrigerant can release heat to the outdoor air and condense into liquid.

You do not need a gas-law formula or pressure calculation here. The practical idea is simple: pressure helps the system choose where refrigerant will boil and where it will condense.

Why does the system keep refrigerant pressure low in the evaporator?

Put it together

Follow the heat through the evaporator.

  1. Warm indoor air reaches the colder evaporator coil.
  2. Heat moves from the warmer air into the colder refrigerant.
  3. Low pressure lets the refrigerant boil at a low temperature.
  4. The refrigerant absorbs latent heat while changing from liquid to vapor.
  5. The air leaves the coil with less heat and feels cooler.
You can now explain: An air conditioner removes and relocates heat. Sensible heat changes temperature, latent heat changes state, and pressure controls the temperature where refrigerant boils and condenses.
